title: Relational Design
description: Master relational database design principles including keys, constraints, and schema patterns used in production systems.

data.text: Relational database design turns real-world requirements into efficient, maintainable table structures. A well-designed schema reduces anomalies, speeds up queries, and makes the data model easy for engineers to reason about. In system design interviews, demonstrating strong relational design shows you understand how to model entities, enforce integrity, and avoid common pitfalls.

Every table needs a primary key—a column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row. Surrogate keys like auto-incrementing integers are simple and performant. Natural keys based on business data like email or VIN can work, but they risk changing over time, which makes updates expensive. In interviews, prefer surrogate keys unless the business key is immutable.

Foreign keys link tables together and enforce referential integrity. A foreign key constraint prevents orphaned rows: you cannot have an order pointing to a non-existent user. When designing relationships, use clear naming conventions such as user_id for foreign key columns so the intent is immediately obvious to anyone reading the schema.

data.text: Constraints protect data quality at the database level. NOT NULL prevents missing values. UNIQUE prevents duplicates. CHECK enforces business rules like price > 0 or status in ('pending', 'paid', 'shipped'). Relying on application code alone for validation is fragile—any client or background job can bypass it. Constraints are your last line of defense.

data.title: Design tip
data.text: Name your constraints explicitly rather than letting the database generate random names. Named constraints make error messages readable and migrations predictable.

Foreign key columns should almost always be indexed. Without an index, every JOIN or DELETE on the parent table triggers a full table scan on the child table. For an orders table with millions of rows, this turns a fast lookup into a slow query. Add indexes early and measure performance later.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use surrogate primary keys unless you have a truly immutable natural key.
Define foreign keys with clear naming conventions and always index them.
Apply NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and CHECK constraints to enforce data quality at the database level.
Good relational design prevents anomalies, simplifies queries, and makes your schema self-documenting.

items.question: Should every table have an auto-incrementing ID?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Junction tables for many-to-many relationships often use a composite primary key from the two foreign keys. However, a single-column surrogate key is simpler for most production tables.

items.question: Are foreign keys required in every relationship?
items.answer: Application-level referential integrity is possible, but foreign key constraints are safer because they cannot be bypassed. Use them unless you have a proven performance bottleneck from cascade checks.
